notes.definition: An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic parts) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same habitat.
explanation: Ecologists describe living things at different levels of organisation. An individual is a single organism. A population is all the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time. A community is all the populations of different species living in that habitat. An ecosystem is the community together with the non-living (abiotic) parts of its environment, such as the soil, water, light and air. A habitat is simply the place where an organism lives.

To survive and reproduce, organisms need a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there. Plants need light, carbon dioxide, water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals need food, water, oxygen and somewhere to live. Because these resources are often in short supply, organisms compete with each other for them. Competition can happen between members of the same species and between different species.

Plants in a community compete with each other for light, space, water and mineral ions from the soil. A tall tree shades smaller plants beneath it, and its roots take up water and mineral ions that other plants could have used. Animals compete with each other for food, mates and territory. For example, red squirrels and grey squirrels compete for the same nuts and seeds, and male deer compete for mates.

Within a community each species depends on other species for things such as food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal. This is called interdependence. Bees depend on flowers for nectar, while many flowers depend on bees for pollination. Birds may nest in trees and spread the trees' seeds. Because species are linked in this way, if one species is removed or its numbers change, it can affect the whole community. For example, if a disease killed most of the rabbits in an area, foxes would have less food, and grass that the rabbits normally ate might grow taller and shade out smaller plants.

A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance, so that population sizes remain fairly constant over time. Examples include tropical rainforests, ancient oak woodlands and coral reefs. Population sizes still go up and down a little, for example in predator and prey cycles, but over many years the community stays much the same. Stable communities usually have a high biodiversity, which makes them less affected by the loss of a single species.

In the exam you may be given charts, graphs or tables showing how the numbers of different organisms in a community change. You need to extract the information (for example, read values from a graph or calculate a percentage change) and then use ideas about competition and interdependence to explain the pattern. Always link a change in one population to a reason, such as more food, less competition or more predators.
keyFacts: An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment.
A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat.
A community is all the populations of different species in a habitat.
Organisms need materials from their surroundings and from other living organisms to survive and reproduce.
Plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions.
Animals compete for food, mates and territory.
Interdependence: species depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.
Removing one species can affect the whole community.
In a stable community, species and environmental factors are in balance and population sizes stay fairly constant.
Examples of stable communities: tropical rainforests, oak woodlands and coral reefs.

keyTerms.definition: The place where an organism lives.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time.
All the populations of different species living and interacting in a habitat.
The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
When organisms try to obtain the same limited resource, such as light, water, food or mates.
The way species in a community depend on each other for things such as food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.
A community in which all species and environmental factors are in balance, so population sizes remain fairly constant.
An area an animal defends from others, usually to secure food or a place to breed.

equations.name: Percentage change
equations.formula: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100

workedExamples.title: Calculating a percentage change in a population
workedExamples.question: A survey counted 240 red squirrels in a forest. Five years after grey squirrels arrived, there were 90 red squirrels. Calculate the percentage change in the red squirrel population.
steps: The negative sign shows a decrease.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the effect of removing a species
workedExamples.question: In a woodland, owls eat mice and mice eat seeds. Suggest what would happen to the seed-producing plants if the owls were removed.
steps: Owls are predators of mice, so with no owls fewer mice are eaten.
Fewer seeds survive to grow into new plants, so the number of seed-producing plants may fall.
workedExamples.answer: The mouse population would increase, so more seeds would be eaten and the number of seed-producing plants would decrease. This shows interdependence.

workedExamples.title: Reading a table of competing species
workedExamples.question: Two species of grass were grown separately and together. Grown alone, species A had a mean dry mass of 12 g per pot. Grown together with species B, species A had a mean dry mass of 5 g per pot. Explain the result.
steps: Compare: 5 g is much less than 12 g.
When grown together the two species compete for the same resources.
Plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions.
Species A got fewer of these resources, so it grew less.
workedExamples.answer: Species A grew less when grown with species B because the two species competed for light, space, water and mineral ions, so species A obtained fewer resources for growth.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a community includes the soil, water and air.
misconceptions.right: In fact a community is only the living organisms (all the populations). Adding the non-living parts makes it an ecosystem.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think competition only happens between different species.
misconceptions.right: In fact organisms of the same species compete too, often more strongly, because they need exactly the same resources.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think animals compete for light and plants compete for mates.
misconceptions.right: In fact plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions, while animals compete for food, mates and territory.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a stable community means population sizes never change.
misconceptions.right: In fact numbers still rise and fall a little (for example in predator and prey cycles), but overall they remain fairly constant over time.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think removing a species only affects the organisms that eat it.
misconceptions.right: In fact, because of interdependence, the effect can spread through the whole community, including to plants, competitors and pollinated species.

realWorld: Grey squirrels, introduced to Britain from North America, outcompeted native red squirrels for food, so red squirrels are now rare in most of England.
The decline of bees threatens crops that depend on insect pollination, such as apples and strawberries, showing interdependence between insects and farming.
Reintroducing wolves to Yellowstone National Park reduced deer grazing near rivers, allowing trees to regrow and changing the whole community.
examTips: Learn the exact lists: plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions; animals compete for food, mates and territory. Do not mix them up.
When asked to explain a population change in a community, follow the chain step by step: what changed, which organism is affected next, and why (more food, less competition or more predators).
Use the word 'interdependence' when a question asks why removing one species affects others, and give a specific dependency such as food, shelter, pollination or seed dispersal.
When reading data, quote values with units and calculate changes or percentages before explaining them.
summary: Ecosystem = community of living organisms interacting with the abiotic environment.
Individual, population, community and ecosystem are increasing levels of organisation.
Plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions.
Animals compete for food, mates and territory.
Interdependence means species rely on each other, so removing one affects the whole community.
Stable communities keep species and environmental factors in balance, so population sizes stay fairly constant.

flashcards.back: Because species are interdependent: others rely on it for food, shelter or pollination, or it controls the numbers of other species.

questions.question: Which term describes all the organisms of one species living in a habitat?
markScheme: 1 mark: population
questions.explanation: A population is all the individuals of one species in a habitat. A community includes many species, and an ecosystem also includes the non-living parts of the environment.

questions.question: Which of these do plants compete with each other for?
markScheme: 1 mark: light
questions.explanation: Plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions. Food, mates and territory are what animals compete for; plants make their own food by photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which statement best defines an ecosystem?
options: The interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment
All the populations of different species in a habitat
The place where an organism lives
All the organisms of one species in an area
markScheme: 1 mark: the interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment
questions.explanation: An ecosystem combines the living community with abiotic factors. Option B is a community, option C is a habitat and option D is a population.

questions.question: Which of these is something male animals of the same species commonly compete for?
markScheme: 1 mark: mates
questions.explanation: Animals compete for food, mates and territory. Mineral ions, carbon dioxide and light are resources that plants need.

questions.question: Which is an example of a stable community?
options: A garden lawn that is mown weekly
A pond that has just been dug
markScheme: 1 mark: a tropical rainforest
questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests, oak woodlands and coral reefs are stable communities where species and environmental factors are in balance. The other options are newly created or regularly disturbed by humans.

questions.question: Bees collect nectar from apple flowers and the flowers are pollinated by the bees. What does this illustrate?
markScheme: 1 mark: interdependence
questions.explanation: Each species depends on the other: bees get food and the apple trees get pollinated. Competition would mean both needing the same scarce resource, and predation would involve one killing and eating the other.

questions.question: Which list is in order from the smallest level of organisation to the largest?
markScheme: 1 mark: individual, population, community, ecosystem
questions.explanation: Individuals of one species form a population; populations of many species form a community; the community plus the abiotic environment forms an ecosystem. Option D is the right levels but in reverse order.

questions.question: Two plant species grow close together in the same soil. Which resource are they least likely to compete for?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen from the air
questions.explanation: Oxygen in the air is plentiful (about 21%), so plants rarely compete for it. AQA lists light, space, water and mineral ions as the resources plants compete for.

questions.question: A disease kills most of the rabbits in a grassland. Which outcome is most likely in the following years?
options: Fox numbers rise because there is less competition between foxes
Grass grows taller and some small flowering plants are shaded out
Grass decreases because fewer rabbits fertilise the soil
Nothing changes because foxes simply eat more grass
markScheme: 1 mark: grass grows taller and some small flowering plants are shaded out
questions.explanation: With fewer rabbits grazing, grass grows taller and competes more strongly for light, so small plants are shaded out. Fox numbers would fall, not rise, because their food supply drops, and foxes do not eat grass.

questions.question: What is the main feature of a stable community?
options: There is only one species present
Species and environmental factors are in balance so population sizes stay fairly constant
There is no competition between organisms
markScheme: 1 mark: species and environmental factors in balance, population sizes fairly constant
questions.explanation: In a stable community numbers stay roughly constant over time. Competition still exists in stable communities, and they usually have many species, not one.

questions.question: Give two resources that animals compete with each other for.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: food, mates, territory (allow water or shelter)
questions.explanation: The AQA list for animals is food, mates and territory. Do not give light or mineral ions, which are plant resources.

questions.question: State the difference between a community and an ecosystem.
acceptedAnswers: ecosystem includes abiotic or non-living factors
markScheme: 1 mark: a community is all the populations of living organisms in a habitat
1 mark: an ecosystem also includes the non-living (abiotic) parts of the environment and their interactions
questions.explanation: A community is only the biotic part. An ecosystem is the community interacting with abiotic factors such as soil, water and light.

questions.question: Name two things that a plant species might depend on an animal species for.
markScheme: 1 mark: pollination
1 mark: seed dispersal
questions.explanation: Many plants rely on insects for pollination and on birds or mammals to spread their seeds. This is part of interdependence.

questions.question: Explain why bluebells growing under a dense beech tree canopy grow and flower mainly in early spring, before the beech leaves open.
acceptedAnswers: more light reaches the ground before leaves open
markScheme: 1 mark: the beech tree competes for light / its leaves shade the woodland floor
1 mark: before the leaves open more light reaches the bluebells for photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Plants compete for light. Bluebells avoid losing that competition by doing most of their growing when the trees are bare, so they can photosynthesise.

questions.question: Grey squirrels were introduced to Britain. Red squirrel numbers have fallen in areas where grey squirrels live. Suggest and explain one reason for the fall in red squirrel numbers.
markScheme: 1 mark: grey and red squirrels compete for the same food (nuts, seeds) or territory
1 mark: grey squirrels are more successful competitors so red squirrels get less food
1 mark: so fewer red squirrels survive and reproduce
questions.explanation: Both species need the same resources. If grey squirrels take more of the food, red squirrels are less likely to survive and breed, so their population falls. (Grey squirrels also carry a virus that harms red squirrels, which is a credit-worthy alternative.)

questions.question: What is meant by the term interdependence? Give an example.
markScheme: 1 mark: species in a community depend on other species (for food, shelter, pollination or seed dispersal)
1 mark: a valid example, for example birds nesting in trees, bees pollinating flowers, foxes eating rabbits
questions.explanation: Interdependence is the network of dependencies between species. Any correct specific example earns the second mark.

questions.question: Competition between individuals of the same species is often stronger than competition between different species. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: individuals of the same species need exactly the same resources
1 mark: for example same food, same nesting sites or territory, same light or mineral ions
1 mark: they also compete for mates, which members of a different species do not
questions.explanation: Different species usually overlap only partly in what they need, but members of one species need identical resources, including mates. So the overlap, and the competition, is greatest within a species.

questions.question: A coral reef contains many species. Explain why a community with many species is likely to be more stable than one with only a few species.
acceptedAnswers: loss of one species has smaller effect
markScheme: 1 mark: species are interdependent
1 mark: with many species, animals have alternative food sources or shelter
1 mark: so the loss or decline of one species has a smaller effect on the rest of the community
questions.explanation: In a diverse community each species is linked to many others, so if one population falls, consumers can switch to other foods and the community stays in balance.

questions.question: A survey found 35 robins, 120 sparrows and 45 blackbirds in a park. How many birds of these three species were counted in total?
markScheme: 1 mark: 200
questions.explanation: 35 + 120 + 45 = 200. Each species is a separate population; together they are part of the park's community.

questions.question: A meadow had 400 bumblebees. After a hedge was removed, a survey found 260 bumblebees. Calculate the percentage decrease in the bumblebee population.
markScheme: 1 mark: 35%
questions.explanation: Change = 400 − 260 = 140. 140 ÷ 400 = 0.35, × 100 = 35%. Dividing by 260 (the new value) gives 53.8%, which is a common error.

questions.question: Wheat grown alone had a mean yield of 8.0 tonnes per hectare. Wheat grown in a field with many weeds had a mean yield of 6.2 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage decrease in yield caused by the weeds. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 23% to 2 significant figures
questions.explanation: 8.0 − 6.2 = 1.8; 1.8 ÷ 8.0 = 0.225; × 100 = 22.5%, which is 23% to 2 significant figures. The weeds compete with the wheat for light, space, water and mineral ions.

questions.question: After wolves were reintroduced to a national park, the number of willow saplings along a river rose from 150 to 420. Calculate the percentage increase.
markScheme: 1 mark: 180%
questions.explanation: Increase = 270. 270 ÷ 150 = 1.8; × 100 = 180%. Wolves reduced deer grazing, so more willows survived: an example of interdependence.

questions.question: A table shows that a population of ladybirds increased when the number of aphids (their food) increased. Use ideas about resources to explain this.
markScheme: 1 mark: more food available so less competition for food
1 mark: so more ladybirds survive and reproduce
questions.explanation: Food is a resource animals compete for. More aphids means more food per ladybird, so more survive to breed and the population grows.

questions.question: In a lake, perch eat small fish and small fish eat water fleas. Anglers remove most of the perch. Which change would most likely happen first?
options: The number of water fleas increases
The number of small fish increases
The number of perch eggs increases
markScheme: 1 mark: the number of small fish increases
questions.explanation: Removing the predator means fewer small fish are eaten, so small fish increase first. Later, water fleas would fall as more small fish eat them, and algae (eaten by water fleas) might then rise. Water fleas would decrease, not increase.

questions.question: Name the level of organisation that includes all the living organisms in a pond but not the water or mud.
markScheme: 1 mark: community
questions.explanation: All the populations of living organisms together make the community. Including the water and mud would make it an ecosystem.

questions.question: A gardener plants lettuce seedlings very close together. Explain why the lettuces grow less well than lettuces planted further apart.
markScheme: Indicative content: plants close together compete with each other; for light (leaves shade each other); for water from the soil; for mineral ions from the soil; for space for roots and leaves; less light means less photosynthesis so less glucose for growth; fewer mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) means less protein made for growth.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clearly explains competition for at least two named resources and links reduced resources to reduced growth.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that the plants compete or names resources, with little explanation of the effect on growth.
questions.explanation: Same-species plants need exactly the same resources. Closely spaced lettuces share limited light, water, mineral ions and space, so each plant gets less and grows less.

questions.question:
In an oak woodland, oak trees provide food (leaves and acorns) for caterpillars, squirrels and jays, and nesting sites for birds. Jays bury acorns, some of which grow into new oak trees. Blue tits eat caterpillars.
A new disease kills a large proportion of the oak trees. Explain how this could affect the woodland community.
markScheme: Indicative content: fewer oak leaves so fewer caterpillars; fewer caterpillars so less food for blue tits, so blue tit numbers fall; fewer acorns so less food for squirrels and jays, so they decline or compete more strongly; fewer nesting sites for birds; jays bury fewer acorns so fewer new oaks grow (seed dispersal lost); more light reaches the woodland floor so ground plants increase; animals that eat ground plants may increase; competition between animals for remaining food increases; the community becomes less stable.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, linked explanation of several chains of effect, using ideas of interdependence (food, shelter, seed dispersal) and competition, including at least one indirect effect.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains two or more effects on other organisms with some linking.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements that some animals would lose food or shelter.
questions.explanation: Strong answers follow each dependency (food, shelter, seed dispersal) to the next organism and add an indirect effect such as extra light helping ground plants. This shows how interdependence spreads one change through a community.

questions.question: Describe what is meant by a stable community and explain why it is important that all the species in a community are in balance.
markScheme: Indicative content: stable community: species and environmental factors in balance; population sizes remain fairly constant over time; examples tropical rainforest, oak woodland, coral reef; species are interdependent; if one population changes greatly it affects food, shelter or pollination for others; this can cause other populations to rise or fall; balance means resources are not over-used.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): accurate description of a stable community with an example and a clear explanation linked to interdependence.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic description, such as populations stay the same, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: A good answer gives the definition, an example, and then explains that interdependence means one big change can disrupt many other populations.
